extracted.intended_audience: health research funders, research policymakers, and researchers studying peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying criteria and practical standards for assessing the effectiveness, fairness, timeliness, and burden of grant peer review systems and for designing improvements. Focus is on peer review for research funding (particularly health sciences) and on evidence-based changes funders might implement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive validity (ability to predict future performance)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is uncertainty in peer review decisions — it is predicting the future — and evidence suggests peer review is not a particularly good predictor, at least for bibliometric performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge and measure uncertainty in decisions; capture and use predictive uncertainty to improve decisions and analyses; recognise limits when using bibliometrics as outcome measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-rater reliability / reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Inconsistency in peer review ratings and mixed evidence on the reproducibility of panel decisions; reliability measures such as the correlation between independent assessors are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure reproducibility explicitly (e.g., correlations between assessors, changes across stages), analyse disagreement levels, and consider them when designing review processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias against innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: The strongest evidence indicates peer review suffers from a bias against innovation (conservatism), disadvantaging novel or high-risk work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design processes that identify and protect innovative work (e.g., portfolio approaches, capture reviewer disagreement as indicator of novelty) and robustly evaluate any interventions intended to reduce this bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive particularism / disciplinary bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers/panel members tend to favour proposals in their own fields or that align with their ways of thinking (termed 'cognitive particularism'); effects may be complex (favoring very familiar or very unfamiliar areas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider broadening the range of fields judged by each group and include diverse fields on panels; balance the benefit of specialist expertise against the risk of particularism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cronyism and conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior affiliation with a reviewer or panel membership is associated with increased chances of funding (evidence of cronyism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain detailed conflict-of-interest processes; consider anonymisation where feasible (evidence mixed); separate expertise effects from nepotism when interpreting patterns; monitor panel member application/award rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence is conflicting: some large-scale studies report no systematic gender bias, others show cohort- or field-specific effects; aggregation over cohorts can create apparent bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for cohort effects and wider systemic factors; interpret meta-analyses carefully; funders may need targeted policies but should evaluate effects empirically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age bias / early career disadvantage
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a small and conflicting evidence base about age bias; early career researchers may be disadvantaged because of fewer preliminary results or smaller portfolios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider policies to equalise success rates for new investigators (e.g., NIH measures), monitor age-related patterns, and evaluate impacts of eligibility rules and support mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field/discipline effects on success
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain fields (e.g., molecular biology) may have higher success rates for grant funding compared to other bioscience fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise disciplinary disparities when designing panels and evaluation criteria; consider panel composition and cross-field representation to mitigate unfair advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of review
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review processes can be slow (9–18 months from submission to funding in many cases) and may hinder research progress and translation; in some contexts (e.g., epidemics) delays can have serious consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate and reduce review timelines where critical (eg triage, expedited review for emergencies), consider system-wide time costs, and study how review time contributes to overall translational delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support and legitimacy among stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite criticisms, peer review retains broad support among academic stakeholders and institutions; perceptions of transparency and objectivity matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure stakeholder confidence and transparency; recognise tensions between protecting reviewer anonymity and showing transparency to applicants; engage stakeholders when trialling reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall burden of peer review (monetised and time costs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The system's burden is increasing. Estimates attribute a large proportion of monetised costs to application preparation (estimates vary widely but often large), with applicants bearing the majority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify burden (monetised and time) across applicants, reviewers, and funders; be cautious when interpreting cost estimates and clearly justify time assumptions; target reductions where they will have most impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of burden (applicants vs reviewers vs funders)
rubrics_metrics.description: Burden falls primarily on applicants (estimates around 74–85% for application production), with reviewers/panel members and administrative costs accounting for smaller shares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise reducing applicant burden or increasing applicant value from applying (e.g., better feedback); when reducing reviewer burden, weigh effects on decision quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application complexity and length
rubrics_metrics.description: Very long and complex applications (e.g., 80–120 pages) increase burden; shortening applications (e.g., to 1,200 words or NIH R01 reductions) has been tried with mixed effects on preparation time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplify application formats but evaluate impacts carefully, since shorter forms do not necessarily reduce applicant preparation time; pilot streamlined formats with before-and-after assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer workload and optimal number of reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer time is a significant cost; studies trade off reproducibility and reviewer burden and suggest optimal numbers (examples: five reviewers optimal in one study; another found 11).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical analysis to set reviewer numbers balancing reliability and burden; consider alternative models (more, shorter reviews vs fewer, deeper reviews).

rubrics_metrics.name: Triage and stage-based review processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Triage of short preliminary applications with high cull rates (e.g., NSF's 75% cull) and multi-stage review can reduce administrative burden but may change success rates and application behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When implementing triage, monitor for unintended consequences (e.g., increased applications, shifting success rates) and evaluate which simultaneous changes drive outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymisation / blinding of reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Blinding reviewers to applicants may reduce some biases, but feasibility and effects are debated and evidence is mixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pilot blinding where feasible, evaluate effects on fairness and decision quality, and consider interaction with proposal length/content (shorter anonymised proposals may differ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer training to reduce bias and improve review quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Some funders have used reviewer training (e.g., CIHR, NIH) to address bias and improve review quality; limited evidence suggests it may reduce discrepancies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement and rigorously evaluate training interventions before large-scale adoption; track effect sizes on agreement and decision outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capturing reviewer confidence and disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should be asked for both a rating and a measure of confidence; levels of disagreement may indicate innovative or contentious work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect confidence measures systematically, analyse disagreement as informative (e.g., flagging potential innovation), and incorporate into selection/portfolio decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of randomness / lotteries for allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce explicit randomness (lottery) within defined fundable pools or two-threshold systems to reduce fine-grained selection errors and bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider lottery approaches to reduce biases and dependency on unreliable fine-grained distinctions; be aware of political challenges; pilot and evaluate (several funders have limited pilots).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative allocation designs (portfolio approaches, two-stage systems)
rubrics_metrics.description: Portfolio selection (funding projects that score highly on different criteria) and two-stage systems (identify best then randomise some funding) are proposed to capture diversity and reduce over-precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design selection strategies that balance diversity, innovation, and robustness; evaluate trade-offs and transparency of complex selection rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology and remote review
rubrics_metrics.description: Technology (remote review, eliminating travel) can reduce time burden and appears not to significantly affect outcomes, but it may reduce side-benefits of face-to-face panels (networking, social interaction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt technologies to reduce administrative burdens while finding ways to preserve or replace networking/side-benefits if they are deemed important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feedback to applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing reviewers' feedback may increase the value applicants receive from applying but may also raise concerns about appeals from rejected applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh benefits of providing actionable feedback against legal/appeal risks; pilot feedback mechanisms and assess applicant-perceived value and administrative costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multimedia proposal formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Altering proposal formats to include multimedia or video has been suggested to improve information transmission and reduce burden, but effects are untested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pilot multimedia formats with careful evaluation of accessibility, equity, review feasibility, and effects on decision quality and burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency, data availability and published evaluations
rubrics_metrics.description: Funders should build in before-and-after comparisons, make data available for analysis, openly publish studies of their processes, and work together on comparative analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require funders to publish evaluation results and underlying data (where appropriate) to strengthen the evidence base and enable independent scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of system-level interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: System changes (amount of funding, researcher demographics) affect peer review, and changes to peer review affect the overall research system; most studies consider parts in isolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study peer review within the broader funding system using modelling/simulation approaches and comparative analyses that account for interacting factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to study panel social processes
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a striking lack of studies examining the social processes occurring during panel discussions, yet these are central to peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funders should cooperate to permit observational studies of panel meetings to understand decision formation and ways to optimise panel discussion processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful evaluation of reforms (before-and-after; publish results)
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes to peer review (e.g., shortened applications, lottery elements, triage, blinding) need careful empirical evaluation since effects are sometimes counterintuitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design reforms with embedded evaluation plans, publish results including negative/null findings, and interpret outcomes in context (e.g., system-level changes occurring simultaneously).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer selection and incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifying appropriate reviewers is a driver of funder burden; experiments (e.g., applicants reviewing each other's grants) can reduce burden but require incentive alignment to avoid manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explore alternative reviewer selection/incentive models with safeguards (e.g., rewarding alignment with group consensus), and evaluate effects on review quality and gaming risk.
